8:["$","$L13",null,{"data":{"chapterId":17,"verseId":5,"chapterTitle":"Examination of Action and Fruit","totalVerses":33,"verseData":{"id":"v17_5","number":5,"title":"Seven Types of Action","sanskrit":{"text":"","transliteration":"","translation":"Virtuous and nonvirtuous actions Derived from pleasure, As well as intention and morality: These seven are the kinds of action."},"philosophy":{"insight":"The opponent completes the classification: seven types of action covering ethical quality (virtuous/nonvirtuous), motivation (pleasure-derived), mental factor (intention), and discipline (morality). This is the comprehensive Abhidharma taxonomy — the opponent's full framework for understanding karma.","madhyamaka":"Seven-fold classification: Various reconstructions exist, but the key categories are ethical quality (kuśala/akuśala), hedonic motivation (kāma-derived), mental volition (cetanā), and moral discipline (śīla). Together, these are supposed to capture ALL types of action and their karmic potential.","quantum":"Complete basis states: in QM, a complete set of basis states spans the full state space — any state can be expressed as a combination of basis states. Similarly, the seven types are meant to span the full \"action space\" — any action fits into this taxonomy.","bridge":"Both QM basis states and Abhidharma action-types attempt complete classification. QM: any state = combination of basis states. Abhidharma: any action = combination of the seven types. Both aim for completeness while (for Nāgārjuna) the classification is conventional, not inherent.","accessible":"Like classifying all animals into categories (mammals, reptiles, etc.), Buddhist scholars classified all actions into seven types. The classification is useful for understanding but doesn't make the categories inherently real — they're conceptual tools.","twoTruths":"Conventionally, the seven-fold classification is a useful teaching tool. Ultimately, the categories and the actions they classify are all empty — conventional designations applied to dependently arisen events.","commonMisconception":"NOT saying classifications are wrong or useless. They're valuable conventional tools. The critique targets treating them as INHERENTLY REAL categories rather than conventional designations."},"quantumResonance":{"concept":"Complete Basis Set Classification","score":52,"strength":"Low","explanation":"QM basis states span the full state space; Abhidharma action-types span the full \"action space.\" Both aim for completeness. Both classifications are conventional/mathematical, not inherently real.","caveat":"QM basis states are mathematical; Abhidharma categories are ethical-philosophical. The parallel is about complete taxonomic frameworks."},"animation":{"visualBridge":"Seven colored streams merging into a single river of karma — each stream represents a type of action, together spanning the full range of human ethical activity.","educationalGoal":"User sees the Abhidharma attempt to comprehensively classify all types of karmic action."},"deeperDive":[{"q":"What are the seven types?","a":"Reconstructions vary, but one version: (1) virtuous speech, (2) nonvirtuous speech, (3) virtuous physical action, (4) nonvirtuous physical action, (5) pleasure-derived action, (6) intention (cetanā), (7) moral discipline (śīla). The exact list matters less than the principle: comprehensive classification.","realLifeExample":"Like classifying food into seven groups (grains, proteins, dairy, fruits, vegetables, fats, sugars). The exact grouping varies; the goal is comprehensiveness."},{"q":"What does \"derived from pleasure\" mean?","a":"Actions motivated by kāma (sensory pleasure) — pursuit of pleasant sights, sounds, tastes, etc. These can be virtuous (sharing a good meal) or nonvirtuous (stealing pleasure) depending on intention and context.","realLifeExample":"Going to a concert (pleasure-derived action). Ethical quality depends on context: supporting artists (virtuous) vs. pirating music (nonvirtuous)."},{"q":"Why does \"morality\" (śīla) have its own category?","a":"Because moral discipline includes both active ethical behavior AND the restraint/avoidance aspects (vows, precepts). It's not just what you DO but what you REFRAIN from doing — a distinct category from action motivated by pleasure or simple intention.","realLifeExample":"A vegetarian's choice to not eat meat is a distinct type of \"action\" (restraint/morality) from actively cooking a vegetarian meal (intentional physical action)."},{"q":"Does this classification exhaust all action types?","a":"The opponent claims yes — the seven types are meant to be comprehensive. Any action can be classified under one or more categories. Nāgārjuna doesn't dispute the comprehensiveness; he disputes the inherent reality of the categories and the actions they classify.","realLifeExample":"A periodic table claims to list all elements. Nāgārjuna isn't saying there are unlisted elements — he's saying the elements listed don't have inherent \"element-essence.\""},{"q":"How does v.5 complete the setup for v.6?","a":"VV.1-5 establish the most detailed conventional understanding of karma. V.6 will ask the devastating question: given all this complexity, how does a CEASED action produce a LATER result? The comprehensiveness of vv.4-5 makes the question of v.6 more pressing — not even the most detailed classification solves the continuity problem.","realLifeExample":"Having the most detailed recipe doesn't explain how the cake gets baked after the oven is turned off. Detailed classification (vv.4-5) doesn't solve the mechanism problem (v.6)."},{"q":"What's the transition from description to analysis?","a":"VV.1-5: descriptive (what karma IS, conventionally). V.6: analytical (HOW does it work, given impermanence?). The shift from \"what\" to \"how\" is where Nāgārjuna's critique begins. Description is easy; mechanism is where inherent existence fails.","deeper":"The shift at v.6 is from phenomenology (describing karma) to ontology (explaining how it works). This is where every non-Mādhyamika school faces its greatest challenge: explaining the mechanism of karmic continuity. Each school proposes different entities (avijñapti, seeds, store-consciousness), but all face the permanence/annihilation dilemma that v.6 articulates. Nāgārjuna's genius is showing the problem is with INHERENT EXISTENCE, not with any particular proposed mechanism."}],"quiz":{"beginner":{"question":"What is the purpose of the seven-fold classification of action?","options":["A) To limit actions","B) To comprehensively categorize all types of karmic action — covering ethical quality, motivation, mental volition, and moral discipline.","C) To prove actions are inherent","D) To deny karma"],"correct":"B","explanation":"The seven types aim to classify ALL karmic actions comprehensively. Any action fits into one or more categories. It's a pedagogical tool, not an inherent ontology."},"intermediate":{"question":"Why doesn't comprehensive classification solve the karma problem?","options":["A) It does solve it","B) Even the most detailed classification doesn't explain the MECHANISM: how does a ceased action produce a later result? Description (vv.4-5) doesn't solve the mechanism problem (v.6).","C) Classification is unnecessary","D) Only simple analysis works"],"correct":"B","explanation":"Classifying actions doesn't explain how they produce results across time. V.6 will raise this fundamental mechanism question."},"advanced":{"question":"Why does the problem identified in v.6 apply to ALL non-Mādhyamika schools?","options":["A) Only one school","B) Because ALL schools face the permanence/annihilation dilemma: if the action persists, it's permanent; if it ceases, how does it produce later results? Every proposed mechanism (avijñapti, seeds, store-consciousness) faces this dilemma.","C) No school faces this","D) Only Mādhyamika has the problem"],"correct":"B","explanation":"The permanence/annihilation dilemma is universal for any account of inherent karmic continuity. Nāgārjuna shows the problem is inherent existence itself, not any particular mechanism."}},"verseText":"Virtuous and nonvirtuous actions Derived from pleasure, As well as intention and morality: These seven are the kinds of action.","madhyamakaConcept":"Seven-fold classification: Various reconstructions exist, but the key categories are ethical quality (kuśala/akuśala), hedonic motivation (kāma-derived), mental volition (cetanā), and moral discipline (śīla).
